meta.system: El Abgadeyya El Maṣreyya (Masri Writing System)
meta.author: Diaa Hassouna
meta.description: Academic tier uses Greek and Coptic letters plus diacritics for sounds Latin cannot represent precisely. Intended for linguistic study and formal documentation.

alphabet.name: Ṯeh
alphabet.notes: Greek theta; Cairene merger → /s/ (Tier 1 uses s or t)

alphabet.name: Jéh
alphabet.notes: Upper Egyptian (Ṣaʿidi) ج — ج صعيدي — also covers the MSA/فصحى pronunciation of ج, and the loanword letter چ; all realized as /ʒ/, contrasting with Cairene ج (see G, hard /g/)
alphabet.notes_ar: ج صعيدي (مصر العليا) — وكمان بتغطي ج فصحى (الفصحى/MSA) وحرف الكلمات الدخيلة چ — كلهم بيتنطقوا /ʒ/، بعكس ج القاهرية (شوف G، جيم قوي /g/)

alphabet.name: Ḥa
alphabet.notes: Coptic Hori; mirrors shape of ح; never numeral 7

alphabet.name: Ḏaal
alphabet.notes: Eth; Cairene merger /ð/→/z/, Masri reflects phonetic reality

alphabet.name: See
alphabet.notes: Restricted to code-switched words kept in original spelling

alphabet.name: Sheen
alphabet.notes: Coptic Shai; dotless ش skeleton; replaces sh digraph

alphabet.name: Ṣaad
alphabet.notes: Emphatic; dot-below rule applies to Ṣ Ḍ Ṭ Ẓ

alphabet.name: Ẓah
alphabet.notes: Merges with Ḍ in most Cairene contexts

alphabet.name: ʿAin
alphabet.notes: Coptic Old Ain; uppercase = lowercase for visual consistency; descends from hieroglyph for 'eye'

alphabet.name: Gheen
alphabet.notes: IPA voiced velar fricative; Extended Latin letter (LATIN LETTER GAMMA, used in the IPA) visually derived from the Greek gamma (Γ/γ), not the Greek Unicode block itself

alphabet.name: Vee
alphabet.notes: Foreign loanwords only; v ≠ f, both original phonemes

alphabet.name: Qaaf
alphabet.notes: Full /q/ for MSA/formal registers; colloquial Cairene → glottal Ɐ

alphabet.name: Heh
alphabet.notes: Soft H as in 'hat'; distinct from pharyngeal Ϩ

alphabet.name: Hamza
alphabet.notes: Upside-down A; glottal stop; mirror of Alef (open ↔ closed); represents ء, ق-Cairene, and all hamza forms (أ ؤ ئ) uniformly; always silent word-initially

vowel_system.rule: Short vowels are optional in fluent writing but required in ambiguous contexts and learning materials.

ayin_rule.title: The ع Problem — Most Critical Rule
ayin_rule.note: In Tier 2, ع is always represented by Ⲵ (uppercase = lowercase for visual consistency).

spelling_rules.name: Gemination (Doubled consonants & Doubled vowels)
spelling_rules.rule: Doubled consonants are written doubled. Doubled vowels are written doubled or single with macron (a → aa, ā).
examples: حُبّ → 7obb / Ϩobb
جدا → geddan

spelling_rules.name: Definite Article
spelling_rules.rule: Always written 'el' regardless of sun/moon-letter assimilation in speech. Spelling consistency is prioritized over phonetic transcription to reduce writer decision load.
examples: البيت → el beet
الشارع → el ϣaareⲴ

spelling_rules.name: Glottal Stop
spelling_rules.rule: Written only mid-word and word-finally, using Ɐ in Tier 2 (apostrophe ' in Tier 1). Word-initial glottal stop — whether etymological ء or Cairene ق — is always silent in spelling and encoded.
examples: أنا → ana (not Ɐana)
مسئولية → masⱯooleya

spelling_rules.name: Digraph Integrity
spelling_rules.rule: Applies to Tier 1 only (sh/kh/gh as inseparable two-letter units). In Tier 2 these are single letters (ϣ, x, ɣ) so this rule is not applicable.
spelling_rules.tier2_note: Superseded by single-character mapping: sh→ϣ, kh→x, gh→ɣ

spelling_rules.name: Cairene ق and Hamza Merger
spelling_rules.rule: Ɐ represents the glottal phoneme regardless of etymological origin. Cairene ق and hamza are treated as a single phoneme (glottal stop) because they are phonetically identical in the Cairene dialect; q is reserved for formal/MSA pronunciation.
examples: بقول → ba'ool (everyday) / baⱯool (Tier 2) — mid-word, so Ɐ is written, unlike the word-initial case in Rule 3
قرآن → Qur'an (formal, retains q)

spelling_rules.name: The Letters P and V
spelling_rules.rule: P and V are full, independent letters, not interchangeable with B or F. p is used mainly in loanwords/modern vocabulary; v is an original, coexisting phoneme.
examples: بيانو → piano (Egyptianized to biano)
بنك → bank
أوفر → over

spelling_rules.name: Negation Suffix Phonology (verb + -sh(i))
spelling_rules.rule: Adding -sh(i) to a negated verb triggers regular, rule-governed vowel changes in the verb stem — written explicitly, the same way the θ→s and ð→z Cairene mergers are, never left to silent guesswork. Three sub-rules: (1) Shortening — a long vowel immediately before a single final consonant shortens when -sh is added. (2) Syncope — a short vowel in the first syllable of the stem may be dropped once -sh is added and the stress shifts. (3) Epenthesis — an unstressed vowel i is inserted when the addition of -sh would otherwise leave the verb ending in a three-consonant cluster. Note: ma itself is written as a separate word (spelling_rules id 10) — these vowel changes affect only the verb+sh(i) unit, not ma.
examples: اختار extaar → ما اختارش ma khtarsh(i) / ma xtarϣ(i) — shortening: long aa shortens before the single final r
كبر keber → ما كبرش ma kbersh(i) / ma kberϣ(i) — syncope: the short e in the first syllable drops
كنت kont → ما كنتش ma kontish(i) / ma kontiϣ(i) — epenthesis: an i is inserted so the word doesn't end kont-sh
spelling_rules.notes: The -sh(i) form (with the historical final i) is the older, now-rare but still correct variant of the same suffix; both -sh and -sh(i) trigger identical stem changes. Confirmed by example that the shortening/elision on extaar still applies even with ma written separately (spelling_rules id 10): الراجل اختار شركة حياته (el raagel extaar shereeket hayaato) vs. الولد ما اختارش لسه الألوان (el walad ma xtarsh(i) lessa el alwaan).

spelling_rules.name: Preposition/Particle + Article Fusion (li/bi/fi/`a/ma + el)
spelling_rules.rule: El is normally a free particle, always spelled separately from the word it modifies (Rule 2). A closed set of short/light prepositions and particles is an explicit exception: li- ("to"), bi- ("by/with/in"), fi- ("in"), the shortened `a-/Ⲵa- (see spelling_rules id 11), and the topicalizing/emphatic particle ma (distinct from negation ma, spelling_rules id 10) all fuse with a following el into a single written word — li-+el→lel (or lil), bi-+el→bel, fi-+el→fel, `a-/Ⲵa-+el→`al/Ⲵal, ma+el→Mal. That fused word then behaves exactly like plain el: it stays separate from the noun that follows it. This is a closed list, not a blanket rule for every preposition — `and ("to have") + el stays two separate words, `and el, never `andel. Negation ma never fuses with the verb it negates regardless of what follows (id 10) — the Mal fusion applies only to the topicalizing ma directly preceding el.
examples: للجامعة (li + el + gāmʿa) → lel gam`a (Tier 1) / lel gamⲴa (Tier 2) — lel stays separate from gamⲴa
بالكتاب (bi + el + kitāb) → bel kitaab / bel kitaab
ف الصميم (fi + el + ṣamīm) → fel ṣamiim (= fuller, unfused fi el ṣamiim)
يللا ع القهوة (yalla + `a/Ⲵa + el + ahwa) → yalla `al ahwa / yalla Ⲵal ahwa (= fuller, unfused yalla `ala el ahwa / yalla Ⲵala el ahwa)
عندي البيت ده (`and + el, NOT fused) → `and el beet da, never `andel beet da
ما المهمة دي لازم تخلص يا حضرات (topicalizing ma + el + mohemma) → Ma el mohemma di laazem texlaṣ ya ϩaḍaraat. (= fused Mal mohemma di laazem texlaṣ ya ϩaḍaraat.)
spelling_rules.notes: lil is an accepted alternate of lel before certain following consonants; both are correct and the choice does not change meaning.

spelling_rules.name: Noun Vowel Shortening Before Suffix
spelling_rules.rule: A medial/final long vowel in a noun shortens before the 'heavier' clitic set — -ha (her), -na (our), -kom (your pl.), -hom (their), and the sound feminine plural suffix -aat — but stays long before the 'lighter' set: -i (my), -ak/-ik (your m./f.), -o (his). This generalizes the verb-side shortening in spelling_rules id 7 to nouns; written explicitly rather than left to silent guesswork.
examples: بيت beet "house": beeti/beetak/beetik/beeto keep the long ee; betha/betna/betkom/bethom shorten it
مراة meraat "wife" (construct) + ha → meratha, not meraatha
مرات meraat "wife" (singular) + aat (sound fem. plural) → merataat "wives", not meraataat
زيت zeet "oil" + na → zetna; دقيق di'ee'/d'ee' "flour" + na → d'e'na / dⱯeⱯna (also shows first-syllable syncope, cf. spelling_rules id 7's kiber→keber)
spelling_rules.notes: Confirmed across two nouns (beet; zeet/di'ee') and the full clitic set — the trigger class is 3rd fem. sg., 1st/2nd/3rd pl., and the plural marker; 1st sg., 2nd sg. (both genders), and 3rd masc. sg. never trigger it.

spelling_rules.name: Negation Particle Separation (ma vs. -sh(i))
spelling_rules.rule: ma is written as its own separate word, the same free-particle treatment as el (spelling_rules id 2) — not fused to the verb. The -sh/-esh/-sh(i) suffix stays glued to the verb (and to any object clitics attached to the verb between the stem and -sh(i)). This mirrors how Egyptian Arabic is written in Arabic script, where ما stands as its own word and ـش attaches to the verb. Avoids producing an overly large single fused cluster for long negated verbs with stacked object clitics.
examples: ماكتبش الواجب ليه؟! → Ma katabϣ(i) el waageb leeh?!
مينفعش → ma yenfaⲴsh(i) — "it doesn't work" (ma separate, verb+sh(i) glued)
معندناش → ma Ⲵndinaaϣ — "we don't have" (ma separate, verb+object-clitic+sh(i) glued)

عليا النعمة ما عملت حاجة! → Ⲵalayya el neⲴma ma Ⲵamalt ϩaaga! — "I swear I didn't do a thing!" (bare ma, no -sh(i) at all — a separate oath/emphatic-register negation pattern, not an abbreviation of ma-...-sh(i))
spelling_rules.notes: Some words with a non-negating 'ma' (e.g. the presentative ماهو ma+huwa) have both a fused everyday pronunciation (mahu) and a fuller separated one (ma ahu) — both are valid; this is a pronunciation-level contraction, not an exception to the negation rule itself. Superseded the earlier fully-fused ma-...-sh(i) treatment.

spelling_rules.name: Preposition Shortening (`ala/Ⲵala → `a/Ⲵa)
spelling_rules.rule: The preposition `ala/Ⲵala ("on, about") can shorten to `a/Ⲵa usually before el and elli (اللي, "which/that/who" — the Egyptian colloquial equivalent of MSA الذي). Both the full and shortened forms are correct. When the shortened `a/Ⲵa precedes el specifically, the two go on to fuse into a single word, `al/Ⲵal — see spelling_rules id 8.
examples: على اللي فات → `a elli faat / Ⲵa elli faat — "about what happened/the past"
يللا ع القهوة (= يللا على القهوة) → yalla `al ahwa / yalla Ⲵal ahwa — shortened `a/Ⲵa then fuses with el (id 8)
spelling_rules.notes: Scope of which following words beyond el/elli trigger the shortening is not yet surveyed.

spelling_rules.name: Loanword phonemic retention vs. nativization threshold
spelling_rules.rule: P and V (Rule 6) are used to preserve /p/ and /v/ in a loanword's citation form — not silently merged to B/F — as long as the word hasn't taken native Egyptian derivational morphology yet. Once a loanword takes native morphology (feminine, plural, verbal derivation), phonological nativization (p→b, v→f) is permitted alongside it, but not required: the citation form and its derived forms are treated as separate lexical entries and may diverge (e.g. pizza keeps p; its derived feminine bitzaya nativizes to b). See masri_loanwords.html §4, §7.
examples: بيتزا → pizza / pitza (citation) vs. bitzaya, bitzat (derived)
فيديو → vidyu, فيترينا → vitrina (v retained even once fully integrated)

spelling_rules.name: Loanword θ→t / ð→d (distinct from the native Cairene merger)
spelling_rules.rule: For loanwords specifically, English/foreign /θ/ and /ð/ are substituted with t and d respectively — not with the native Cairene merger targets s and z (θ→s, ð→z) used for the Classical Arabic ث/ذ letters. These are two different substitutions and must not be conflated: one governs native ث/ذ spelling, the other governs how a borrowed th-sound is heard and spelled by Egyptian speakers.
examples: ترمس (thermos) → tarmas, not tarsas

spelling_rules.name: ˈʃˈ and ˈŋˈ in loanwords — no new letters; ˈʒˈ reuses J
spelling_rules.rule: Masri Tier 2 does not add dedicated letters for /tʃ/ or /ŋ/. /tʃ/ is written as the two-letter sequence t+ϣ where retained, simplifying to plain ϣ in fully nativized forms. /ŋ/ is written as plain n before a following velar consonant, the same allophonic treatment n already gets in native words — not a distinct phoneme in Egyptian Arabic. /ʒ/ is the one exception: Masri already has a letter for it, J (shared with native Ṣaʿidi/MSA ج), so a retained loanword /ʒ/ may use J directly; otherwise it defaults to ϣ, or to g in older, already-nativized French-origin loans that historically hard-g'd — decided by the nativization threshold, not by guessing a word's age.
examples: جراج (garage, old French loan) → garaaj (ʒ→g)
سندوتش (sandwich) → sandawitsh (tʃ retained) vs. شيبسي (chips) → ϣibsi (tʃ→ϣ, fully nativized)
باركينج (parking) → parking (ŋ written as n before k)

spelling_rules.name: Consonant clusters and stress in loanwords
spelling_rules.rule: Word-initial and word-medial consonant clusters that don't occur natively are retained as pronounced by default, not broken up with an inserted vowel — unlike ordinary Egyptian phonotactics. An epenthesized variant is only recorded when it's itself an attested common pronunciation, never invented by rule. Stress is not marked orthographically for loanwords, the same as for native words.
examples: بلاستيك (plastic) → plastik, initial pl- retained
بلوزة (blouse) → blooza, initial bl- retained

spelling_rules.name: Canonical loanword spelling vs. accepted variant vs. wrong
spelling_rules.rule: Every loanword sense gets exactly one canonical Tier 2 spelling, matching its dominant attested Cairene pronunciation. A second attested pronunciation is recorded as an explicit accepted variant (slash-separated), never as a silent alternative. A hypothetical respelling nobody actually says is marked wrong, not merely omitted. This formalizes the convention already used in loanword_examples below.
examples: بيتزا → pizza / pitza (canonical + accepted variant); bizza marked wrong
باسبور → passport / passpour (canonical + accepted variant); bassport / basboor marked wrong

sample_texts.tier2_academic: Ana baϨeb Maṣr. El ahwa el maṣreyya aϨsan ahwa fi el donya. Keda miϣ ra'y, dah ϨaⱯiⱯa.
sample_texts.tier1_everyday: Ana baheb Masr. El ahwa el masreya ahesan ahwa fi el donya. Keda mesh ra'y, dah ha'i'a (haqiqa).
sample_texts.arabic_script: أنا بحب مصر. القهوة المصرية أحسن قهوة في الدنيا. كدة مش رأي. دة حقيقة.
stress_test_sentences_tier2: Ana Ⲵarif inno el loɣa el maṣreya aϨsan loɣa fi el donya, we da elli xallāni aϣtaɣal feha koll yoom.
El ott el adeem baⲴdeen ge el beet we Ϩabbeto geddan — howa el waϨeed elli miϣ meⲴaⱯadni.
Bass lamma Ϩawwelt aṭbaⲴ el awraaⱯ el mohemma kanet el printer miϣ ϣaɣɣala lel asaf Ⲵaϣan el power cable miϣ mawgood.
El ḍabⲴ da ẓahar ṭabⲴan we el mawḍooⲴ da etⲴaⱯad xalaaṣ.
Inϣāllāh bokra nϣūf, elϨamdillāh Ⲵandena waⱯt.
El moϣkela en el ϣaɣɣāla el xeϣna el ɣaϣeema el over ɣalaṭatha ziyāda fe el θamarāt.
We ewⲴa el ouda elli goowa el beet el beeⱯa elli fi el ϣaariⲴ el mahgoor laϨsan hatexsar keteer.
ForⱯoⲴlowz raⱯaṣ Ⲵa el sellem we bass keda ya sidi we el meⲴallem Sardeena dafaⲴ feloos keteer lel ṣowaan we el farsha Ⲵa el ard.
Oom oⱯaf we enta betkallemni, Oom oⱯaf boṣṣeli we fahhemni.
EϨna benⱯool aaxer madena heyya madenet el Salaam ya abo el Ⲵorréf, matlaɣweϣϣi Ⲵalayya we balaaϣ avwara ya over enta.

design_principles: Regular sound-to-symbol correspondence: Masri aims for a highly regular correspondence between speech sounds and written symbols, with explicit orthographic rules — not silent exceptions — governing the contextual, morphological, and lexical cases where a sound and a symbol don't map one-to-one (e.g. the θ→/s/ and ð→/z/ Cairene mergers, the ق/ء glottal-stop merger, and gemination).

Orthography over phonetics where the two conflict: some Masri spellings preserve lexical or morphological identity rather than surface pronunciation (for example, the definite article is always written 'el' regardless of sun/moon-letter assimilation in speech). That is a deliberate orthographic choice, not a claim about how the word is actually pronounced.
Simplicity prioritized over aesthetics: speed and ease over formal elegance.
Cairene reference dialect: urban Cairo Egyptian Arabic is the normative standard.
No numerals: no Arabic or Western numeral substitutes a letter.
Keyboard accessibility (Tier 1): everyday symbols typeable on standard Latin keyboards; Tier 2 requires supplementary Greek/Coptic input.

Hijaʼi letter order: the alphabet follows the common hijaʼi order of Modern Standard Arabic, with minimal modification. Extra letters not present in MSA (P, V, J, C) are inserted immediately beside their nearest phonetic or graphemic relative rather than reordering the whole system: P after B, V after F, J after G (both represent ج), and C after S.

origin_legend.ASCII: Standard ASCII characters, no special input needed
origin_legend.Latin_ext: Ð (U+00D0); emphatics Ṣ Ḍ Ṭ Ẓ (dot-below rule); Ɐ (U+2C6F)
origin_legend.Extra: C and J — extra letters added beyond the common MSA hijaʼi set. C is restricted to code-switched spelling (/s/, /k/). J covers Upper Egyptian (Ṣaʿidi) ج, MSA ج, and the loanword letter چ — all /ʒ/, distinct from Cairene ج (hard /g/, see G).
